title: Road To Damascus Cashbox
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Source row: BARMATRIX Q# 19554, Criminal Law and Procedure, Property Crimes, common-law classification; credited classification is larceny.

Final Christian variation — QID 19554_road_to_damascus_cashbox

Lydia owns a private Bible-themed escape room called Road to Damascus. For one evening, she assigns Peter to the entry table for the “shipwreck puzzle” room. Peter may take visitors’ $18 admission fees and drop the bills through the slot of Lydia’s wooden ark-shaped cash box. During his shift, Peter pulls $360 from the box and hides it in his costume satchel, intending to keep it.

Call: What is the best common-law classification?

---
call: What is the best common-law classification?

choices.A: False pretenses, because the visitors handed the admission fees to Peter voluntarily.
choices.B: No theft offense, because Peter was allowed to handle the admission money.
choices.C: Embezzlement, because all theft by a worker from the business is embezzlement.
choices.D: Larceny, because Peter had custody of the admission money while Lydia’s business retained possession.

rightExplanation:
D is correct. Peter was only a table worker collecting admission money for Lydia’s business and putting it into her cash box. The best common-law classification is larceny because the worker had custody of the cash while the business retained possession.

Gold Key: Low-level workers who merely handle the owner’s cash usually have custody, not lawful possession. Pocketing that cash is larceny, not embezzlement.

Silver Key: In a theft-classification array, do not start with the job label. Sort the property path: custody, possession, title, or no offense.

---

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text: False pretenses is a neighboring property-crime frame. The voluntary handoff fact does not answer title-by-deception to Peter.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: Permission to handle is not permission to keep. This is a wrong-element answer.

c3.label: CUT C
c3.text: “All theft by a worker” is an overclaim. It tries to classify by role instead of property relation.

c3.label: CALL / Anchor confirmation
c3.text:
D survives only with the Gold Key: custody is not lawful possession. Low-level custody plus pocketing is larceny.

---

studentScript: Call: classify the theft. Cut C because all-worker theft is overbroad. Cut B because handling is not keeping. Use the Gold Key to cut A and keep D: custody plus owner possession equals larceny.

A.signal: The choice points to voluntary payment, but the call asks Peter’s classification after he pockets business money.
A.lawyer: False pretenses requires title obtained by deception; the visitors paid Lydia’s business, not Peter personally.

B.signal: The answer proves only that Peter could handle the money; the stem says he hid it intending to keep it.
B.lawyer: Limited authority to handle cash does not authorize appropriation.

C.signal: The word all makes the answer too broad.
C.lawyer: Worker theft can be larceny when the worker has custody rather than lawful possession.

D.signal: Matches the Gold Key: custody with owner-retained possession.

goldKeys.statement: A low-level worker who merely handles the owner’s cash usually has custody, not lawful possession. If the worker pockets it intending to keep it, the common-law classification is larceny.
goldKeys.trigger: Worker is authorized to collect or handle money for the owner, then secretly pockets it.
goldKeys.unlocks: Larceny versus embezzlement in low-level worker cash cases.
goldKeys.authority: Lawyer-confirmation only: common-law larceny and embezzlement authorities.

remediation.title: Custody is not possession
remediation.studentMove: Ask whether the worker had custody only, lawful possession, title by deception, or no taking.
